Human-Centric Digital Twin Ecosystems for smart environments

This research develops human-centric Digital Twin ecosystems for Industry 5.0 by enabling adaptive interaction between humans, robots, and smart environments. The project integrates Human Digital Twins, AI/ML, XR, robotics, and motion tracking technologies to support safer and natural collaboration in manufacturing and beyond. Applications include cobots, drones, humanoids, healthcare, and assistive environments, with emphasis on adaptability, collaboration, and explainable human-aware systems.

About the position:
Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) is seeking a motivated full-time PhD student to contribute to research on Human-Centric Digital Twin Ecosystems for smart environments and Industry 5.0 systems. The project focuses on developing adaptive Digital Twin and Human Digital Twin technologies that improve collaboration between humans, robots, and intelligent environments in a safe, efficient, and human-centred way.
The research explores how Digital Twins can support real-time interaction between people, robotic systems, and smart infrastructures. Beyond monitoring users, the goal is to create adaptive systems capable of learning from human behaviour and adjusting robotic actions, workflows, and environments accordingly. Applications include collaborative robots, drones, mobile and humanoid systems, XR technologies, and smart environments in manufacturing, healthcare, and assistive domains.
The student will work with AI/ML, robotics, XR, IoT systems, motion capture, and simulation tools to develop intelligent and user-aware Digital Twin solutions. Particular focus will be placed on collaborative and multi-user environments where humans and robotic systems interact together dynamically. The research will also investigate explainable and long-term Human Digital Twins that adapt to user behaviour, support skill development, improve safety, and enable more natural human–robot interaction.
The position combines research, experimentation, and practical implementation. The student will contribute to software development, experimental validation, scientific publications, project activities, laboratory support, demonstrations, and selected teaching and supervision activities within an international and interdisciplinary research environment.

Doctoral Positions in Robot Learning and Soft, Musculoskeletal, and Biohybrid Robotics
The Soft Robotics Lab within the Institute of Robotics and Intelligent Systems at ETH Zurich is inviting applications for several doctoral positions. Our lab's goal is to build, model, and control robots in a fundamentally different way, so that they become more flexible, dexterous, capable, and adapt better to their environment. We work along four directions: soft and musculoskeletal robotics, biohybrid living systems, dexterous manipulation and robot learning, and simulation for embodied AI. We are looking for exceptional candidates in any of them. This round we especially want two profiles: people who design and build the robots, and people who make policies run on them.

We do not hire against a narrow project description. Your thesis topic is something we shape together in your first months. Tell us which of our directions pulls at you, and what you would want to build.

Project background
Today's robots are mostly rigid, fragile, and a world apart from the agility and resilience of biological bodies. Our bet is that the next generation of robots will be soft, musculoskeletal, and in part alive. They will be built to make contact with the real world rather than to avoid it. We pursue this across four directions, and a strong candidate will find a home in one of them and borrow from the others.

Soft and musculoskeletal robotics. We build bodies from compliant structures, bones, joints, and tendon-like actuation. Our electrohydraulic musculoskeletal leg jumps, moves fast, and adapts to terrain at roughly 1.2% of the energy a motor-driven leg needs ( Nature Communications, 2024 ). Our low-voltage HASEL actuators run near 1100 V, are safe to touch, and work untethered and underwater ( Science Advances, 2024 ). We recently extended these muscles to full antagonistic motion ranges ( ICRA 2025 ) and to a sensorless, inherently compliant anthropomorphic hand driven entirely by electrohydraulic actuation ( IROS 2026 ).

Biohybrid living systems. We grow engineered muscle and use it to actuate machines. We bioprinted multicellular muscle-tendon units that transmit force along a real musculoskeletal path ( Science Advances, 2025 ), embedded sensors directly into muscle for closed-loop control of proprioceptive biohybrid robots ( Advanced Intelligent Systems, 2025 ), and established functional volumetric bioprinting with xolography ( Advanced Materials, 2026 ). Co-optimized volumetric muscle designs for large dynamic deformations are in press at Nature Communications (Balciunaite et al., 2026). The same fabrication line reaches clinical work: with University Hospital Zurich we printed implantable reinforced cardiac tissue patches ( Advanced Materials, 2025 ).

Dexterous manipulation and robot learning. We build hands and the policies that run them. One of our initial hand designs is now commercialized through our spin-off Mimic Robotics . ORCA is our open-source, reliable, and cost-effective anthropomorphic hand for uninterrupted dexterous task learning ( IROS 2025 ). On that hardware we work on imitation learning and diffusion policies, cross-embodiment skill transfer through latent action diffusion (ICRA 2026), sample-efficient reinforcement learning and policy fine-tuning directly on the real robot , vision-language-action models for contact-rich tasks, and tactile representation learning on our high-resolution sensorized skin (ICRA 2024). We also build controllable dexterous world models for training and evaluation, and a benchmark of dexterity for anthropomorphic hands . Whichever side you come from, the offer is the same: the hand, the skin, the simulator, and the people who designed all three sit in one room. Build a mechanism here and someone will have a policy running on it within weeks. Build a policy here and you can change the mechanism when the mechanism is what is wrong.

Simulation, fabrication, and embodied AI. Building these robots requires tools that did not exist. Vision-Controlled Jetting prints rigid skeletons, soft tissue, tendons, and sensors in one pass, including a full musculoskeletal hand and forearm ( Nature, 2023 ). We close the sim-to-real gap with learned residual physics ( RA-L, 2024, Best Paper Award ), and we released SORS , a modular high-fidelity soft-robot simulator, at RoboSoft 2026.

Underwater and aerial systems run through all of this, from SoFi and tendon-driven swimmer digital twins to our open-source soft aerial manipulation platform ( CoRL 2024 ).

Job description
Depending on your direction, your work will emphasize different parts of the following. All of it happens in a lab where hardware, biology, and learning sit in the same room.

You will take a research idea from concept to a working system: designing the architecture, building it, integrating sensing and control, and validating it through systematic real-world experiments

If your focus is systems design, you will design and build the robots themselves: mechanisms and compliant structures, actuators and tendon routing, embedded electronics and motor control, and the sensor integration that makes a machine measurable. You will own a system from CAD through fabrication to hardware that still runs six months later

If your focus is learning, you will develop policies and perception that run on real, compliant, contact-rich hardware: imitation learning, real-world reinforcement learning and fine-tuning, sim-to-real transfer, and multimodal representations that use touch as well as vision. You will help define the benchmarks that make such claims measurable

Each design cycle feeds the next, so rapid prototyping, measurement, and iteration sit at the heart of every project

Drawing inspiration from biological musculoskeletal systems, you will engineer how bones, joints, tendons, and muscles can be recreated with compliant materials, artificial actuators, or living tissue, and how their interplay produces strength, dexterity, and robustness

You will build robots that derive much of their capability from their embodiment, achieving rich, adaptive behavior with less reliance on complex centralized control

If your focus is biohybrid systems, you will work in our biological laboratories at ETH, culturing and bioprinting tissue and turning it into a controllable actuator

You will publish at the top venues in the field, release open-source hardware and code where it helps the community, and present your work internationally

You will supervise semester and Master's projects, which is how most of our doctoral students learn to lead work, and you will collaborate day to day across our hardware, muscles, and machine learning teams

You will complete a doctorate at ETH Zurich alongside the research, including the coursework of the D-MAVT doctoral programme and a share of teaching in one of our courses

Doctoral Student in Neuromotor Interfaces for Dexterous Robot Teleoperation (multimodal egocentric vision + EMG)
The Sensing, Interaction & Perception Lab  invites applications for a fully funded PhD position at ETH Zürich at the intersection of robotics, wearable sensing, signal processing, machine learning, and human-computer interaction.

The goal of this PhD is to develop neuromotor interfaces for dexterous robot teleoperation using two sensing modalities:

1)  surface electromyography (sEMG) measured at the wrist or forearm, with the aim of decoding subtle hand and finger activity, continuous movement, and motor intent in real time.

2) egocentric vision as a complementary input channel.

While EMG provides information about human motor intent, egocentric cameras can provide context about the surrounding scene, manipulated objects, hand–object interactions, and task state. Combining these modalities creates opportunities for interfaces that understand both what the user intends to do and what is happening in the environment.

The PhD will focus on the computational and sensing methods required to make such systems robust, generalizable, and effective in real interactive settings, including multimodal learning and reasoning across neuromotor and egocentric visual signals , while exploring applications in Mixed Reality and other interactive systems.

Particularly beneficial: You have a background in (or experience with) prototyping sensing systems ( embedded systems , signal acquisition, processing, PCBs)

Note: This is not a position in biomedical engineering and there is no health focus.

Project background
Wearable EMG provides a direct and unobtrusive way to sense muscle activity underlying hand and finger movements. This creates opportunities for interfaces that can recognize subtle actions, continuously estimate movement, and infer motor intent before or without large observable movements.

Making such interfaces work reliably outside controlled settings remains a substantial research problem. EMG varies across users and recording sessions and is sensitive to electrode placement, contact conditions, movement, and other sources of noise. This motivates research in signal processing, temporal machine learning, representation learning, adaptation, and real-time inference.

A second challenge is that neuromotor signals alone provide limited information about what the user is interacting with and why a particular movement is occurring. The project will therefore combine EMG with egocentric vision to capture objects, hands, contacts, affordances, and task state. This creates a multimodal research problem: learning representations that combine neuromotor and visual information and developing methods for reasoning about human intent, hand–object interaction, and the state of an ongoing manipulation task.

For robotic teleoperation, these multimodal signals can support systems that jointly reason about what action the user intends, which object or target the action refers to, and how that intent should be translated to a robot with a different embodiment. Relevant problems include dexterous manipulation, shared autonomy, multimodal intent inference, and reasoning over sequences of human and robot actions.

Job description

Develop signal-processing and machine-learning methods for multichannel EMG, including discrete and continuous decoding of hand and finger activity

Develop egocentric computer-vision methods for understanding hands, objects, hand–object interactions, contacts, affordances, and task state

Develop multimodal learning and reasoning methods that combine EMG with egocentric vision to infer motor intent and interaction context

Investigate reasoning over objects, actions, interaction sequences, and task state to resolve ambiguous motor signals and anticipate intended actions

Apply methods to  dexterous robot teleoperation , including mapping human motor intent to robot manipulators and dexterous hands

optionally:

Prototype wearable sensing systems , including electrode configurations, signal acquisition, embedded processing, and hardware and software integration (huge plus)

Develop and evaluate applications in robotics, Mixed Reality , and other interactive systems

and as in each PhD

In our research group, we design mechanically robust, multi-responsive polyurethane elastomer with backbone-integrated molecular switches. Our aim is to move beyond conventional stimuli-responsive materials, which merely switch between predetermined states, toward life-like materials that genuinely learn: Forming memories, consolidating them over time, selectively forgetting, and adapting their behavior through experience, all while retaining commercial-grade mechanical properties.
In this PhD project, you will synthesize and characterize semi-crystalline polyurethane elastomers containing backbone-integrated photo-, halo-, and thermochromic molecular switches, and investigate how their interactions can be engineered to produce quantifiable memory and learning behaviors.

PhD position in the development of life-like materials that learn, remember, and forget for use in soft robotics
Your tasks
Synthesize libraries of single-, dual-, and triple-switch polyurethanes (Stenhouse salt, DASA, and Spiropyran) via copolymerization and post-polymerization functionalization, and validate backbone integration by NMR, GPC, DSC, DMA, tensile testing, UV-Vis spectroscopy, and pump probe characterization.
Design and characterize synergistic switching cascades (collaborative, competitive, and interdependent pathways) using time-resolved and spatially resolved spectroscopy, patterned illumination, and pH/thermal stimuli.
Develop and validate logic maps for memory formation, consolidation, and selective forgetting, and translate these into training-recall-forgetting cycles on physical polymer films and bilayer actuators.
Contribute to integrating learning materials into soft robotic bilayer actuators and, together with the wider team, demonstrate behavioral adaptation in autonomous soft robots.
Collaborate with international partners

Your profile

We are looking for a highly motivated, curious person who enjoys working at the interface of synthetic chemistry, materials science, and soft robotics, who is comfortable in a multidisciplinary, collaborative environment. Doctoral position in robotic spraying for biocementation
The Chair for Digital Building Technologies invites applications for a PhD position on robotic spraying as an additive manufacturing process for biocementation. The research brings together two closely coupled lines of work: the development of an additive robotic fabrication system based on material deposition and microbially induced calcium carbonate precipitation (MICP), with a focus on applying MICP to the fabrication of architectural elements.

This PhD is part of the SNSF-funded project “DFabuLis: Digital Fabrication Using Living Systems”, conducted in collaboration with Dr. Dimitrios Terzis, Senior Scientist in the Laloui group at EPFL.

Project background
Conventional cement-based construction binds aggregates through an energy-intensive process. Bio-binders offer a different fabrication logic. In biocementation, certain bacteria precipitate calcium carbonate between particles, allowing binding to form under ambient conditions. This project treats the bio-binder as a fabrication parameter. Through robotic deposition of bacterial and cementation solutions, mineral binding can be spatially controlled across a printed structure, producing architectural elements with locally differentiated density, strength, porosity, and surface properties within a single component.

The research will investigate how robotic deposition of biocement can be translated into architectural production strategies, from material placement and component geometry to surface formation and assembly. In collaboration with the Soil Mechanics Laboratory at EPFL, the project connects robotic fabrication with the characterisation and formulation of bio-binders. The resulting strategies will be explored in architectural-scale demonstrators.

Job description

You will develop a robotic fabrication process for biocementation, including adapting existing deposition hardware, and the computational workflow linking design intent to material placement

You will use it to produce architectural components, investigating through making how graded biocementation can inform structure, surface, and assembly

You will assess the environmental footprint of the process and use it to guide fabrication and design choices

You will conduct research in close collaboration with project partners at ETH and EPFL and, where applicable, industry partners.

You will work closely with the Soil Mechanics Laboratory at EPFL, whose characterisation of the material will inform the development of the process

You will write scientific articles for publication in peer-reviewed journals, present at international conferences, and contribute to teaching through the supervision of semester and master's projects

Introduction
Are you eager to study how workers can shape the AI and robotic systems they use, so that technology helps them to improve their quality of working life and their performance? We are looking for a PhD candidate to become part of a multidisciplinary research programme on digital technology and work.
Job Description
The project
AI and robotics can help workers handle demanding tasks, yet their actual benefits depend on how technologies are selected, introduced and adapted in everyday work. Workers may have too little say in those choices or face an overwhelming number of decisions without adequate support. The Design work package of the NWA-project AUGMENT therefore asks when, how and to what extent workers themselves should be able to decide how technology supports their work. Its goal is to develop evidence-based guidance for worker-augmenting technology implementation across small and large organizations and among workers with different educational backgrounds. Thus, your work will directly contribute to a future of work wherein technology augments rather than replaces human work.
Your research will connect work and organizational psychology, work design, human-technology interaction and participatory design. You will examine which forms of assistance workers need, which technologies can meet those needs, and which job decision opportunities allow workers to adjust technology while sustaining their job quality, well-being and performance. The precise research questions and studies will be refined with the supervisory team and consortium partners.
Your role in this project
Within this project, you will:
Conduct fieldwork and collaborate with practical and knowledge workers in small and medium-sized and large organizations, by - among others - performing task and capacity analyses and interviews about their experience of work and desired support.
Review relevant AI and robotic applications, interview technology integrators, and help assess their potential to support workers using an available human-machine synergy scoring approach.
Develop and use a transportable laboratory setting at TU/e to study simulated work activities and decisions about AI and robotics
Design a longitudinal field study of how workers use decision opportunities over time and their implications for labour productivity and meaningful work.
Analyse qualitative and quantitative data, develop practical guidance for job redesign with partner organizations, and communicate findings to workers, organizations and other stakeholders.
Publish scientific papers, present at international conferences, and complete a doctoral dissertation.

Your research will be embedded in the Human Performance Management (HPM) group of the School of Industrial Engineering at TU/e. HPM develops scientific knowledge and tests theories that uncover and explain (psychological) processes contributing to performance at the organizational, team, and individual level. By examining the ‘people factor’ in operational and innovation processes, HPM aims to ensure that employees can help in bringing organizational strategies to fruition in the most rewarding and efficient way possible. See:  https://www.tue.nl/en/research/research-groups/industrial-engineering/human-performance-management for more information about HPM research.
Prof. Dr Pascale Le Blanc (TU/e) is the assigned promotor; your co-promotors are Dr. Anna-Sophie Ulfert-Blank (daily supervisor, TU/e) and Dr. Milan Wolffgramm (daily supervisor, Saxion). Dr. Paul Preenen (Saxion) will serve as scientific advisor. You will closely collaborate with partner organizations and theoretical and practical workers involved in the NWA-project AUGMENT.
The wider AUGMENT consortium connects research on changing work, worker agency, technology design and implementation. Thus, this PhD position offers ample opportunities to work across disciplines, collaborate actively with organizations and researchers from different institutes, and translate research into meaningful guidance and tools for practice.

What happens when the Internet fails?
What happens when a submarine cable is cut? When satellites lose contact with one another? Or when a cyberattack disrupts the networks we depend on every day? The Internet is remarkably resilient, but it is far from invulnerable. As our dependence on digital infrastructure grows, so does the need to understand where it is vulnerable, how failures spread, and what we can do about them.
These are some of the questions we want to explore in RESILIOUS.
We are bringing together 15 PhD researchers and a network of universities, research centres, and industry partners across Europe to investigate how we can make the Internet more resilient. The research spans satellite communications, underwater robotics, network security, autonomous systems, and Internet governance. As part of RESILIOUS, you'll have the opportunity to explore challenging research questions, experiment with new ideas, and work alongside researchers and industry experts from different disciplines and countries. We are recruiting 15 PhD students. If you are curious about how the Internet works, why it sometimes fails, and what we could do differently, have a look at our open positions. One of these questions might be yours to explore.
The 15 PhD Positions offered are as follows:
DC1 — Can satellite networks stay connected when things go wrong?
DC2 — What if satellites from different operators could talk to each other?
DC3 — Can we make the Internet more resilient by rethinking how networks connect?
DC4 — Doctoral candidate in predictive robotic inspection for resilient undersea cable infrastructure
DC5 — How can we detect cyber anomalies in space systems?
DC6 — How close is too close when satellites meet in orbit?
DC7 — What are our options when satellite navigation stops working?
DC8 — Could mobile networks help us detect drones in the sky?
DC9 — Can we hear a maritime threat before we can see it?
DC10 — Can satellite networks autonomously adapt their routes when conditions change?
DC11 — Can we predict when a communication link is about to degrade and proactively mitigate its impact on connectivity?
DC12 — How can context-aware knowledge enable autonomous network self-healing?
DC13 — How do underwater networks stay connected when links disappear?
DC14 — Who decides how the Internet should work?
DC15 — Can the Internet become fragile because of how it is governed?

Job requirements
We welcome applications from curious and motivated people from around the world. You don't need to know everything about your chosen research topic before starting your PhD. We're looking for people who enjoy tackling difficult problems, asking questions, learning new things, and working with others. Different positions call for different skills and backgrounds, so have a look at the individual vacancies to see which ones interest you.
Eligibility requirements
There are a few formal requirements under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) programme:
No PhD yet : You must not already hold a doctoral degree at the time of recruitment.
Mobility rule : You must not have lived or carried out your main activity (work or studies) in the country where you will be recruited for more than 12 months during the 36 months before recruitment. MSCA exceptions may apply.
Open to all nationalities : You can apply regardless of your nationality.
University admission : You must meet the PhD admission requirements of the university associated with your position.

About the programme
The 15 PhD positions are offered within RESILIOUS (Building Europe’s Internet Resilience for a Connected Future), a European Doctoral Network funded by the European Union under the Horizon Europe Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA). TU Delft is one of the participating institutions in the RESILIOUS project and co-coordinates the recruitment process. Two of the available PhD positions will take place at TU Delft.
Conditions of employment
The MSCA allowances follow the EU contribution for MSCA Doctoral Networks [ link ] coefficient applied per country [ link ]. Please note that the net salary will be calculated by deducting these contributions and any other applicable national taxes (e.g., income tax) from the gross amount. For an accurate expectation ensure you check your estimation during the selection process.
A total of 15 PhD researchers will be recruited within this project and appointed at participating universities, research centres, and industry partners across Europe. Employment conditions, including net salary, benefits, duration, and other contractual arrangements, will depend on the host institution or employer. The employment conditions of the respective university, research centre, or industry partner will therefore apply.
Conditions of employment TU Delft
If you will be appointed at TU Delft you will be offered a 4-year period of employment in principle, but in the form of 2 employment contracts. An initial 1,5 year contract with an official go/no go progress assessment within 15 months. Followed by an additional contract for the remaining 2,5 years assuming everything goes well and performance requirements are met. Hence the duration of the PhD project will be 4 years in stead of the standard 3 years funded by the MSCA project.
Salary and benefits are in accordance with the Collective Labour Agreement for Dutch Universities, increasing from 3.204 to 4.051 euro gross per month, from the first year to the fourth year based on a fulltime contract (38 hours), plus 8% holiday allowance and an end-of-year bonus of 8.3%.
As a PhD candidate you will be enrolled in the TU Delft Graduate School. The TU Delft Graduate School provides an inspiring research environment with an excellent team of supervisors, academic staff and a mentor. The Doctoral Education Programme is aimed at developing your transferable, discipline-related and research skills.
The TU Delft offers a customisable compensation package, discounts on health insurance, and a monthly work costs contribution. Flexible work schedules can be arranged.
Will you need to relocate to the Netherlands for this job? TU Delft is committed to make your move as smooth as possible! The HR unit, Coming to Delft Service , offers information on their website to help you prepare your relocation. In addition, Coming to Delft Service organises events to help you settle in the Netherlands, and expand your (social) network in Delft. A Dual Career Programme is available, to support your accompanying partner with their job search in the Netherlands.

About your research statement
We are not looking for a polished research proposal or a summary of everything you know about the topic. We'd like to understand how you approach an unfamiliar research problem. Choose one specific question related to the position and explain why you find it interesting, what makes it challenging, and how you might begin investigating it. We would also like you to describe one assumption you would question or one experiment that might prove your initial idea wrong. There is no single correct answer. You are welcome to use AI tools to help with writing and language, but the research choices and reasoning should be your own. We may discuss your ideas during the interview. You can address your application to Anna Gralka.

Are you curious about how we can squeeze every bit of efficiency out of vehicles and make transport more sustainable? Do you enjoy turning equations, data and code into real-world impact? Chalmers University of Technology is recruiting two doctoral students in vehicle energy estimation to do cutting-edge research at the intersection of engineering, data science, and uncertainty quantification. One position is in mechatronics, at the Department of Electrical Engineering. The other is in vehicle dynamics, at the Department of Mechanical Engineering.

You will join a large, friendly academic community where asking "why?" one more time is seen as a strength, not a problem. Chalmers is a research-intensive university with a strong focus on engineering, natural sciences, and sustainable development. The environment is international, open, and collaborative, and the project includes partners from research institutes, vehicle manufacturers, and system suppliers.

What you will do

In the REACH  project, two doctoral students will work side by side to model, estimate, and predict vehicle energy use in real traffic. You will help us understand where the energy goes, how much can be saved, and how confident we can be in our estimates.

PhD position 1 – Mechatronics (Department of Electrical Engineering)

You will model the loads that drive energy consumption, such as rolling resistance and aerodynamic drag, and how they vary under real driving conditions.

PhD position 2 – Vehicle dynamics (Department of Mechanical Engineering)

You will study how uncertainty in input data, such as the predicted speed profile ahead, propagates into the overall energy estimate, and develop methods to quantify and reduce it.

In both positions, you will:

Develop and evaluate models for vehicle energy consumption and efficiency

Analyse experimental, field and fleet data to understand real-world energy use

Design and run simulations and estimation algorithms using model-based and/or data-driven methods

Work closely with supervisors, other doctoral students, and partners in industry and research institutes

Present your work at international conferences and in scientific journals

Contribute to teaching and supervising students, corresponding to approximately 20% of full-time

Along the way, you will build solid skills in scientific methods, communication and collaboration.

Who you are

You like the idea of spending a few years going deep into one topic, learning a lot and sharing that knowledge with others. You enjoy solving complex problems step by step, and you are not afraid of equations, code, or getting stuck on a tricky bug before you finally crack it. You are also a team player who likes to discuss ideas and build on other people's perspectives.

To thrive in either position, you likely have:

A master's degree (or equivalent) in mechanical, electrical or vehicle engineering, engineering physics, applied mathematics, or a related field

Strong skills in mathematics and in modelling dynamic systems

Experience programming in at least one language, for example Python or MATLAB

An interest in vehicles, transport, energy systems or sustainable mobility

Good spoken and written English for everyday teamwork and scientific communication

You are welcome to apply for one or both positions. Please state in your cover letter which position(s) you are applying for.

About us

The project spans two departments at Chalmers, and each department will host one doctoral student.

Department of Electrical Engineering – Division of Systems and Control (position 1)

The Department of Electrical Engineering conducts research and education across a broad range of fields, from machine learning, signal processing, and information and coding theory to automatic control and electric power engineering. It is an international environment with close ties to both academic and industrial partners. As a doctoral student in mechatronics, you will join the Division of Systems and Control , whose research covers automatic control, automation, and mechatronics. The division works on societal challenges such as energy efficiency, sustainable battery use, safety in autonomous vehicles, and helping industry stay competitive through smart automation.

Department of Mechanical Engineering – Division of Vehicle Engineering and Autonomous Systems (position 2)

The Department of Mechanical Engineering combines technology, people and society to drive the transition to a sustainable future. Through research, education and collaboration, the department creates solutions that link materials to mobility and ideas to impact. As a doctoral student in vehicle dynamics, you will join the Division of Vehicle Engineering and Autonomous Systems , whose research covers vehicle analysis and robotics. The division works on transport systems that combine safety, energy efficiency, driving experience, artificial intelligence and automation across road, rail, aviation and maritime transport.

What we offer

As a Doctoral student at Chalmers, you are an employee and enjoy all employee benefits. Read more about   working at Chalmers   and our  benefits  for employees.

A dynamic and inspiring working environment in the coastal city of Gothenburg .

Read more about Sweden’s generous parental leave, subsidized day care, free schools, healthcare etc at Move To Gothenburg.

Chalmers is dedicated to improving gender balance and actively works with equality projects, such as the GENIE Initiative for gender equality and excellence .

If Swedish is not your native language, Chalmers offers Swedish courses to help you settle in.

Find more general information about doctoral studies at Chalmers here .

Your development and support

During your doctoral studies, you will work closely with supervisors who support both your research and your broader development. You will have access to courses and training in research methods, teaching, communication and leadership, giving you a solid platform for many different future career paths. You will also be part of a wider network of doctoral students who share both the challenges and the fun parts of research life.

If you join us from abroad, you will find a welcoming international community and plenty of support in settling in, both at work and outside it. The university offers Swedish language courses for international staff, which makes it easier to integrate into daily life and collaborate more widely over time.

Project description
Third-cycle subject: Production engineering
We are seeking a motivated PhD student to develop AI and robotic methods for adaptive manufacturing systems, with a particular focus on agentic and embodied AI. The research addresses how robots and intelligent production systems can perceive changing conditions, reason about process requirements and constraints, and adapt their actions in real time. The project brings together task level decision intelligence, multimodal perception, digital twin based learning and robot control to enable more flexible and intelligent manufacturing.
The research will use battery assembly and disassembly as application scenarios.
The PhD student will develop and experimentally validate AI enabled robotic methods in these scenarios, while addressing research questions that are relevant to a broader range of adaptive manufacturing systems.
The position is part of a joint PhD program between KTH and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU). The PhD student will be full time employed at KTH and spend at least 12 months at SJTU, distributed across several research stays. Upon successful completion of the joint PhD programme, KTH and SJTU will jointly issue the PhD degree, with reference to the national accreditation authorized for each university.

Project description
Third-cycle subject: Industrial Economics and Management
The deployment of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has expanded rapidly across public and private sectors. AI-driven technologies—particularly machine learning algorithms and large language models —are becoming integral to knowledge creation, task augmentation, and business analytics. This shift has catalyzed a rise of AI ecosystems, which brings together AI startups, intermediaries, and established enterprises, fundamentally reshaping how employees, businesses, and entire industries function. However, while certain use cases offer efficiency gains, organizations frequently grapple with critical challenges, such as low returns on investment, output unreliability, and pressing ethical dilemmas.
This PhD project aims to critically analyze the organizational implications of AI. The PhD student may explore questions such as, but not limited to: How do organizations mitigate the managerial challenges stemming from the probabilistic nature of AI technologies? How will AI transform the modern industry; and what are the opportunities and risks associated with such transformation? Along with the Big Tech companies and AI giants, what role do startups and intermediaries play in a more responsible transformation towards AI-based economy?
The PhD position is a part of the Wallenberg AI, Autonomous Systems and Software Program - Humanity and Society (WASP-HS), a national research program in Sweden. WASP-HS fosters novel interdisciplinary knowledge about AI and autonomous systems and their impact on humanity and society. WASP-HS enables cutting-edge research, expertise, and capacity building in the social sciences and humanities. For more information, see here .
